why: Scoped to the three top-level scripts (mutate.py 251, pointers.py 474, skills_sync.py 692 = 1417 lines); tools/audit/mutations already has its own record dated 2026-07-25. The classification half has no equivalent and the comparison half has several, so a single verdict for the directory would be a lie either way. Nothing found reports the two cases that actually cost this repo working checks: a hook settings.json EXECUTES whose entire file content is a path to another machine (pointers.py:212-218, kind wired-hollow, which the docstring at pointers.py:20-34 rates worst precisely because the wiring looks complete), and a skills-tree entry that is a 38-byte FILE where a directory belongs whose real body sits in a sibling tree (skills_sync.py:129-134 plus locate_body at 149-185, which ranks usable/deadpath/hollow so the report names a repair rather than a defect). Standard symlink tooling is verifiably blind to both here: `git config --get core.symlinks` returns false on this repo and `git ls-files -s | awk '$1=="120000"'` returns 0 rows, while state/tmp-pointers.tsv holds 38 pointer rows -- the links were flattened into ordinary regular files before they were ever committed, so find -xtype l, the symlinks(1) utility, and git's own file mode all report nothing. But the repo-vs-live half of skills_sync.py does not survive the same test. Running `diff -rq dot-claude/skills ~/.claude/skills` on 2026-07-29 produced 71 lines -- 59 'Only in' and 11 'Files ... differ' -- which is repo_only, live_only and drift in one command with nothing installed; chezmoi covers the same ground with a maintained MIT binary whose `verify` exits 1 when the destination does not match the source; and BOTH recurse into a skill's subdirectories while skills_sync.py hashes only SKILL.md (skills_sync.py:242-251), so a drifted script inside a skill directory reads as in sync. That diff run proved the gap live by reporting `Only in dot-claude/skills/azure-runtime: __pycache__`, a real difference our own checker cannot report. So: keep pointers.py, keep mutate.py's harness guards, keep skills_sync.py's classify/locate_body/squat semantics, and hand the set-diff-and-copy core to diff -rq or chezmoi.

alternatives.name: chezmoi (twpayne/chezmoi, chezmoi.io) -- dotfile manager, source tree in git -> destination in $HOME
alternatives.covers: The entire repo-to-live half of skills_sync.py, and for the whole dot-claude tree rather than skills alone: `chezmoi apply` is cmd_deploy, `chezmoi add` is cmd_import, `chezmoi diff`/`status` is the drift block, `chezmoi verify` is cmd_check (confirmed at chezmoi.io/reference/commands/verify: exit 0 when all targets match their target state, exit 1 when they do not), and `chezmoi unmanaged` lists destination files it does not manage, which is the live_only case. Its comparison table confirms Windows support and that it materializes real FILES, not symlinks -- the correct model for this machine.
alternatives.gap: No notion of a skill body being hollow: no line-count classification (skills_sync.py:100-120 splits pointer <=3 body lines / thin <40 / real), no DEAD_PATH regex for /home/*, /mnt/*, ~/.codex/ (skills_sync.py:65), and no 'a FILE sits where a directory belongs' check -- chezmoi would treat each 38-byte pointer file as a legitimate managed file and deploy it, which is exactly the silent no-op skills_sync.py:31-36 exists to refuse. It also has no locate_body sibling-tree search, so it cannot tell a squatter that needs a copy from one that needs a deletion. And it does nothing at all for pointers.py: `chezmoi doctor` diagnoses chezmoi's own configuration, not whether a hook named inside dot-claude/settings.json resolves to a file (pointers.py:160-186).
alternatives.cost: A new Go binary in a repo that is stdlib-Python-only end to end. Migration means renaming the committed tree into chezmoi's source-state convention (dot_claude/, private_, etc.), which touches far more than tools/audit. CI value is near zero: a GitHub runner has no live ~/.claude, which is why ship-gate.yml:133-134 already runs only `skills_sync.py selftest` and never `check`.
alternatives.maturity: Verified 2026-07-29 by fetching github.com/twpayne/chezmoi: MIT licence, 20.9k stars, Windows listed among supported platforms; and chezmoi.io/comparison-table: implementation language Go, single binary, Windows support yes, dotfiles are Files. NOT verified: latest release version, its date, or release cadence.

alternatives.name: diff -rq / rsync --dry-run --itemize-changes / Unison (already-present or one-install file comparison)
alternatives.covers: The three-way set diff, for free. Executed here on 2026-07-29: `diff -rq dot-claude/skills "$HOME/.claude/skills"` returned 71 lines, 59 'Only in <side>' and 11 'Files ... differ', which is exactly survey()'s repo_only + live_only + drift buckets. rsync -n --delete --itemize-changes gives the same in machine-readable form. Unison adds bidirectional conflict detection on top. All three recurse into subdirectories, which skills_sync.py's SKILL.md-only comparison (skills_sync.py:242-251) does not.
alternatives.gap: Names only, no meaning: no severity, no hollow/thin/real classification, no dead-path detection, no squat detection, no locate_body ranking, and no exit-code contract beyond 'differences exist' (skills_sync.py:307-316 distinguishes default from --strict, where hollow only counts under strict). Unison additionally introduces a 'last successful sync' archive, a notion this job does not have and does not want -- there is no authoritative last sync, only a committed side and a live side. None of them touch pointers.py's or mutate.py's job.
alternatives.cost: Zero for diff and rsync: both are already on this machine via Git Bash and were used to produce the numbers above. Unison is an extra install and a state directory.
alternatives.maturity: diff and rsync are POSIX-era stable and are not the failure point. Unison is described as actively maintained in the 2026 tutorials found; I did NOT verify its release cadence or current version.

alternatives.name: GNU Stow (and dotbot, yadm, rcm -- the symlink-farm family listed at dotfiles.github.io/utilities)
alternatives.covers: Would make repo-vs-live drift structurally impossible rather than detectable, by symlinking the committed tree into ~/.claude instead of copying it. If adopted, cmd_deploy, cmd_import, the sha comparison and the whole drift block become unnecessary rather than replaced.
alternatives.gap: Actively contraindicated on THIS machine, and the reason is the component's own subject matter. `git config --get core.symlinks` returns false here (verified 2026-07-29), and search confirmed that a Git checkout with core.symlinks=false writes a symlink out as a plain text file containing the target path -- which is precisely the shape of all 38 pointer rows pointers.py currently reports. Adopting a symlink-farm model on a Windows checkout is adopting the mechanism that produced the defect. Stow is also Perl and POSIX-oriented with no Windows story; chezmoi's own comparison table is what pushed me to check this.
alternatives.cost: Zero install on Linux, wrong platform here. dotbot and yadm carry the same symlink assumption; yadm's templating was reported in the comparison sources as depending on external tools that became unmaintained, which I did NOT independently verify.
alternatives.maturity: Stow is long-established and stable. I did NOT verify per-project release cadence for Stow, dotbot, yadm or rcm.

alternatives.name: kcchien/skills-cli -- a CLI specifically for managing Claude Code and Claude Desktop skills
alternatives.covers: The closest DOMAIN match found anywhere: same file layout, same product, and the same house constraints (Python 3.10+, stdlib only, MIT, cross-platform). Its commands are list / installed / install / remove / validate / doctor / pack / sync, so `installed` addresses 'what is actually deployed' and `validate` addresses 'is this skill well formed', which together cover part of skills_sync.py's committed-versus-deployed question.
alternatives.gap: Per its README (fetched 2026-07-29) the model is git-repo -> install, recording source repo, commit hash and install time. The README does NOT describe a byte-level both-directions drift report between a local committed tree and ~/.claude/skills, an import of live-only skills back into the repo (skills_sync.py:365-407), or any hollow/squat/dead-path classification. Its metadata-based staleness check would also be blind to a skill edited in place under ~/.claude, which is the exact failure skills_sync.py's sha comparison catches. I did NOT install or run it, so what `validate` and `doctor` actually assert is unverified beyond the README summary -- this is the alternative most likely to be underrated by this record.
alternatives.cost: The lowest-cost adoption on this list: MIT, Python stdlib only, no new runtime. It would still not remove pointers.py or mutate.py.
alternatives.maturity: 58 stars and 30 commits on the main branch at fetch time. The page I fetched did not show a most-recent-commit date or any release, so current activity is UNVERIFIED -- treat as small and possibly dormant, not as dead.

alternatives.name: lychee (lycheeverse/lychee) -- async link checker for Markdown, HTML and text
alternatives.covers: The doc-ref third of pointers.py (pointers.py:244-264, currently 38 of the 76 findings in state/tmp-pointers.tsv). It checks links in local files, accepts globs, and has --root-dir for resolving relative paths plus fallback-extension probing, and ships a GitHub Action so it is CI-ready.
alternatives.gap: It resolves LINKS. pointers.py's CONFIG_REF (pointers.py:64-68) deliberately matches BARE absolute paths written in running prose -- ~/.claude/..., /home/x/..., /c/Users/x/..., C:\Users\x\.claude\... -- with no markdown link syntax around them, which is how every one of the 38 current doc-ref hits is written. It also applies an msys-to-Windows translation and a ~ expansion before testing existence (pointers.py:78-92), without which a live /c/Users hook path reports as broken on this machine. lychee does neither, has no severity model, and has no concept of settings.json hook wiring at all.
alternatives.cost: A Rust binary, a Docker image, or a GitHub Action. Free.
alternatives.maturity: Actively maintained on the evidence found: current docs site (lychee.cli.rs), a maintained lychee-action, and a published Docker image. I did NOT verify a version number or release date.

alternatives.name: find -xtype l / the symlinks(1) utility (mckern/symlinks) / git's own mode 120000
alternatives.covers: The canonical, textbook answer to 'find a link that points at nothing': `find . -xtype l`, `symlinks -r <path>` which classifies dangling / relative / absolute / messy / other_fs, and `git ls-files -s` filtered to mode 120000 for every path git itself believes is a symlink.
alternatives.gap: Verified inapplicable to this repo, which is the whole reason pointers.py's pointer class exists. `git ls-files -s | awk '$1=="120000"' | wc -l` returns 0 here on 2026-07-29 while state/tmp-pointers.tsv holds 38 pointer rows, several tagged 'basename matches, so this was a link that got flattened'. There is no symlink left to walk: the flattening happened before the commit, so the artefacts are ordinary regular files whose content happens to be one absolute path. No symlink-aware tool can see a file that is no longer a link, and none of them has the discriminator at pointers.py:140-148 that separates a path from `/usr/bin/env python3 x.py`.
alternatives.cost: Zero. find and git are already here.
alternatives.maturity: find and git are not the failure point. The standalone symlinks(1) utility's current maintenance was NOT verified.

alternatives.name: mutmut / cosmic-ray / universalmutator (generic mutation testing, for mutate.py:1-251)
alternatives.covers: Automatic mutant generation and kill-rate reporting. universalmutator is structurally closest because it accepts an arbitrary shell command as the kill-oracle, which is exactly mutate.py's 'run the target's own selftest' model.
alternatives.gap: The argument was made in docs/prior-art/tools-audit-mutations.json on 2026-07-25 (targets expose a bespoke argparse `selftest`, not pytest; 0 test_*.py outside the vendored .venv) and I did NOT re-verify those tools' current release cadence this session. What that record did not defend, and what belongs here, is the DRIVER's harness guards: a mkdir-based concurrency lock because two runs write per-index mutants into the same directory and would silently grade each other's leftovers (mutate.py:81-111), a refusal to pass a spec that declares zero mutations (mutate.py:123-129), an abort when the UNMUTATED copy is not green so no later 'caught' can be misattributed (mutate.py:132-147), a rule that a find-string matching other than exactly once is UNGUARDED rather than skipped (mutate.py:155-161), and a three-way grade of each kill as named-[FAIL]-check versus crash versus bare-nonzero (mutate.py:172-192). A generic AST mutator reports killed/survived and none of those distinctions.
alternatives.cost: Adding pytest plus a mutation framework to a repo with no test framework today, to replace a 251-line driver whose specific guards would have to be rebuilt on top.
alternatives.maturity: NOT re-verified this session. The 2026-07-25 record cites mutmut v3.3.1 and a cosmic-ray release dated 2026-04-02; treat both as stale until rechecked.

alternatives.name: A `requires:` field in SKILL.md frontmatter, validated by a schema check (for skill_deps.py)
alternatives.covers: The correct shape of the problem. A declared dependency list is precise, needs no regex, cannot over-report, and would let a skill state a requirement it never writes as a command, such as an API the model is told to call or a data store assumed present. This is what a package manager does and it is strictly better information than grepping.
alternatives.gap: The field does not exist in the Agent Skills format and no skill in any of the four trees on this machine declares one, so a validator for it would today validate 0 of 182 skills. It also cannot be retrofitted by anyone except each skill's author, and a large share of our tree is vendored from upstream repos we do not control. Grepping invocations is the only method that works on skills as they actually exist today.

alternatives.covers: Discover, compare, inspect, review, create, improve, repair, install, sync and rate SKILL.md folders. On its own description it is the closest external thing to skill_deps.py, and it is on the shortlist in the same analysis that produced this amendment.

It is also a skill, meaning it runs when a model chooses to invoke it, whereas a gate domain needs a command that exits non-zero.

what_ours_does:
Three independent tools that all answer one question -- is this check real, or does it only look real. pointers.py (474 lines) walks dot-claude / dot-codex / dot-agents plus a settings.json and emits four classes at three severities (pointers.py:20-34): wired-missing (settings.json runs a hook, no file there, pointers.py:205-209), wired-hollow (the hook exists and its entire content is a path, rated worst because the wiring looks complete, pointers.py:212-218), pointer (any file whose whole body is one unresolvable absolute path, pointers.py:224-238, with a 'basename matches, so this was a flattened link' note at 233-237), and doc-ref (a document naming a ~/.claude, ~/.codex, /home/*, /c/Users/* path not on this machine, pointers.py:244-264). It is strict about what it will call a pointer: <=400 bytes, one line, no shebang, no shell metacharacters, and a rule at pointers.py:140-148 that a whitespace-separated token containing no path separator is an ARGUMENT, so `/usr/bin/env python3 x.py` is a script rather than a pointer. win() at pointers.py:78-92 translates msys /c/Users to a Windows path before testing existence but deliberately refuses to translate /home/*, and normalize() at 269-282 collapses the spellings of one home directory so 40 references to one absent file are counted as one problem rather than 40. --fail-on turns severity into a real gate (pointers.py:334-338), and the selftest (pointers.py:341-443) plants one of each kind AND four must-not-fire cases (a real script, a one-line command with arguments, a pointer whose target does exist, a doc naming a live path) plus three severity-threshold assertions. It explicitly refuses to repair anything (pointers.py:36-41): a pointer does not record what the file used to contain, so writing a replacement would be inventing a file and calling it a fix. skills_sync.py (692 lines) measures dot-claude/skills against ~/.claude/skills in both directions at once and grades each name: repo_only, live_only, drift, hollow (a SKILL.md of <=3 body lines, or <40 lines contaminated by a /home/*, /mnt/* or ~/.codex/ path, skills_sync.py:65,100-120), no_manifest, and squat -- a FILE where a skill directory belongs, which is why an entry count of 63 was once read as 63 skills (skills_sync.py:22-29,129-134). For each squatter, locate_body (skills_sync.py:149-185) searches the LIVE tree, dot-agents and dot-codex in preference order and returns usable / deadpath / hollow per candidate, because absence and unusability call for different repairs; that distinction is a documented regression -- an earlier version dropped every unusable candidate and printed NOWHERE for seven names that had 20-plus lines of real procedure in dot-codex. Hollow skills are excluded from the deployable set rather than counted as gaps, and fail only under --strict (skills_sync.py:309-310). cmd_deploy and cmd_import (skills_sync.py:333-407) copy in either direction and then RE-SURVEY FROM DISK rather than asserting on what they think they wrote (354-361, 399-405); copy_skill's isfile branch (319-330) exists because copytree raises FileExistsError on a squatting pointer file, which would have failed on exactly the ten names that most needed importing. Its selftest (skills_sync.py:439-657) runs 15+ planted cases including a deliberately CLEAN pair, so a pass carries information. mutate.py (251 lines) loads a spec by file path (not import, because tools/ is not a package, mutate.py:50-64), writes each mutant BESIDE its target rather than in a temp directory (mutate.py:25-31: several targets resolve their repo root from __file__, and a %TEMP% copy would turn every case BROKEN and every mutation falsely 'caught'), and grades kills three ways at mutate.py:172-192 -- caught by a named [FAIL] check, caught by a crash with later checks unrun, or caught by bare nonzero -- printing the last two as WEAK SIGNAL. It holds an atomic mkdir lock (mutate.py:81-111), refuses a spec declaring zero mutations (123-129), aborts when the unmutated copy is not green (132-147), and reports a find-string matching zero or 2+ times as UNGUARDED rather than skipping it (155-161).

AMENDED 2026-08-06, fourth tool. skill_deps.py (356 lines) asks the one question the other three do not: can a skill that is present, tracked and in sync actually START on this host. It regex-matches named invocations of 15 binaries and 12 commercial products in each skill's own text, probes this machine (shutil.which for binaries, filesystem traces for products, no network and no auth attempt), and emits runnable / blocked / unbound per skill with the literal matching snippet carried on every blocked row. It was built because the operator asked for skill recommendations that would not repeat the Linear/Notion/Obsidian mistake, and the first run turned the question inward: 26 of 71 committed skills name a binary or product absent here, az is not installed at all while the gastown registry routes an entire Azure persona at eight owned skills, and dot-agents/skills/obsidian-vault is routed while pointing at a vault path that does not exist. Every one of those passes pointers.py and skills_sync.py unremarked, which is exactly the split this record already argues for: same directory, same 'looks real, is not' family, different axis. The detection method is a grep and it over-reports: hand-grading the first 26 downgraded 15 (ten are `bun test` inside a JavaScript workflow, five are prose mentions, including jira-task-draft whose own text says it never calls the Jira API), and an earlier run flagged voice-metrics as needing Notion and Obsidian because its 200,000-line English lexicon contains both words. The snippet on each row exists so that grading is possible and auditable, and the errors run in the cheap direction, since a false block costs a manual downgrade while a false pass is a skill that dies at first use. Detection is a floor on blockage, never a ceiling.

AMENDED 2026-08-06, fifth tool. persona_audit.py (249 lines) moves the same question up a level: skill_deps asks whether one skill can start, this asks whether a persona the router names can do anything at all. It parses the gastown registry for personas and owned skills, resolves each skill across the three payload trees and the live tree, reads the persona's declared tools out of its agent frontmatter, and classifies operational / write-blocked / routed-dead. Measured before the repair: 98 owned skills, 95 resolving in the repo, 23 loading live, 7 personas with zero live skills, 3 owning a file-producing skill with no Edit or Write tool, 0 spawns ever recorded, and all three corpus paths the registry names absent from the machine. The mechanism was a tree mismatch the existing tools could not express: the registry was authored against dot-claude/skills and dot-agents/skills while the runtime loads ~/.claude/skills, and skills_sync.py measures exactly that drift and exits 0 on it. After deploying and promoting, 0 routed-dead and 0 write-blocked. Producer detection is a curated set of skill names rather than an inference, so write-blocked is a floor and not a ceiling, the same honesty limit skill_deps carries.

AMENDED 2026-08-06, sixth tool. pile.py (298 lines) is the reconciliation half. skills_sync keeps parallel trees in agreement; the operator asked the opposite, to merge them, because parallel trees are how one skill drifts into three versions. pile.py refuses to merge and instead emits the manifest a merge needs: duplicate document groups and cross-tree skill groups, each split into byte-identical (collapse is free) versus forked (collapse destroys work), each naming a PROPOSED survivor under a stated rule with every candidate carried. Measured: 51 duplicate document groups covering 58 redundant copies, all collapsed against the manifest; 29 identical skills and 29 forked ones across the three payload trees, the forks left for a human because review is 22k in dot-agents against 11k in dot-claude and heidegger-reflect 29k against 3k. Its sharpest lesson is a guard rather than a count: the first run proposed deleting dot-codex/AGENTS.md because it is byte-identical to the root CLAUDE.md, which would have silently unconfigured the Codex runtime, so PROTECTED_BASENAMES now states that identical bytes at a runtime path are placement and not waste.
strongest_counterargument: The split I recommended is the comfortable half of the truth. The harsh version: skills_sync.py's 692 lines largely exist to produce a prettier `diff -rq`, and the one it produces is WORSE. It hashes only SKILL.md (skills_sync.py:242-251), so every other file in a skill directory -- scripts, references, assets -- is unchecked, and today's diff run demonstrated that live by reporting a subdirectory difference our own `check` cannot see. The 15-case selftest at skills_sync.py:439-657 is the best code in the file and most of it is regression-locking a set comparison that a one-line shell command already does correctly and more completely. The honest aggressive verdict is adopt for skills_sync.py: let `diff -rq` or `chezmoi verify` produce the name sets, and shrink the bespoke part to a classifier that takes those names and answers hollow / thin / real / squat / where-does-the-body-live. That deletes cmd_deploy and cmd_import (skills_sync.py:333-407) whose distinctive property -- copy, then re-survey from disk instead of trusting the write -- chezmoi apply followed by chezmoi verify also provides, plus sha, listdirs and the survey set arithmetic; a rough read puts that at 350-450 of the 692 lines, though I did not attempt the port and that number is an estimate, not a measurement. I stopped short of adopt for two reasons that a future session should weigh rather than inherit: nobody has run chezmoi against this tree, and the CI story is genuinely different (a runner has no ~/.claude, so this check is local-only either way, which caps chezmoi's marginal value). But 'split' understates the size of the deletion, and this record must not be re-read as a defence of all 692 lines. A second, smaller version of the same complaint applies to pointers.py: 38 of its 76 current findings are doc-ref, the lowest-severity class, which lychee plus a grep for bare ~/.claude paths would substantially cover, and its two high-severity classes have been at zero since the tree was cleaned -- a check that has found nothing for a quarter is a check whose value is asserted rather than observed, which is precisely the standard this repo applies to everything else.
